name: Notre-Dame Cathedral
short_description: Medieval cathedral on Ile de la Cite, one of the finest examples of French Gothic architecture

beats.script_body: Beneath Notre-Dame's chancel, vestiges of a pillar-shaped monument dedicated to Jupiter were found in 1711 — the Pilier des Nautes, erected by the corporation of water merchants (Nautae Parisiaci). Inscriptions date it to the reign of Emperor Tiberius (AD 14-37), making it the oldest sculpted monument found in the capital. The merchants engraved their own gods alongside those of Rome. The pillar is now displayed in the Musee National du Moyen Age at the Hotel de Cluny.
beats.source_passage: vestiges of a pillar-shaped monument dedicated to Jupiter, found in 1711 under the cathedral's chancel
beats.fact_check_notes: Tiberius reign corrected from AD 17-34 to AD 14-37.

beats.script_body: Between 1163 and 1330, anonymous artisans carved Notre-Dame from stone, slipping imperceptibly from the Romanesque to the Gothic style yet sustaining architectural unity. Bishop Maurice de Sully initiated the project, commissioning a monument to transcend every other in the kingdom.
beats.source_passage: Between 1163 and 1330, man's yearnings for the divine were carved into her stone

beats.script_body: Notre-Dame hosted only two coronations, both controversial: Henry VI of England, who had conquered France, and Emperor Napoleon. The legitimate French dynasties always used the cathedral of Reims. Henri IV's conversion to Catholicism was celebrated here in 1593 with a Te Deum, though the conversion ceremony itself took place at Saint-Denis.
beats.source_passage: only two coronations, both controversial: that of Henry VI of England who had conquered France and that of the Emperor Napoleon

beats.script_body: In Rabelais's tale, the giant Gargantua visited Notre-Dame and, followed and gawked at by Parisians, climbed the church tower and urinated on the crowd below, drowning 260,418 people (exclusive of women and children). In Rabelais's version, the city of Lutetia became known as Paris — from 'par rie' (for a laugh) — in recognition of Gargantua's jest.
beats.source_passage: Rabelais's hero Gargantua naturally went to Notre-Dame during his visit to Paris

opening_hours_basis: Gated cathedral you enter through doors; hours since the 2024 reopening not confidently known; left unfiltered.
visit_basis: The west facade with its portals and towers, plus the parvis and views from around the Ile de la Cite, absorb 25 minutes; the interior nave, chancel, rose windows and side chapels take around 35 minutes plus an entry queue since reopening.
judgement_basis: A cathedral interior demands silence and stillness so children cannot run and normal conversation is discouraged, and the surrounding parvis is open paving without quiet free seating; the Ile de la Cite location is lit and trafficked with people about, so being left standing after dark is fine.
queue_basis: Since the post-fire reopening entry is managed through a controlled single access point with high demand, forming a substantial line to walk into a free cathedral that eases only at opening and near closing.

anchors.label: The west front
anchors.basis: The whole facade — rose window, gallery and the row of kings together — is only visible from well back: a person STANDS on the parvis paving, sixty to eighty metres out, near the kilometre-zero star, and walks backwards until it fits (W7.11, 11/11: 45 m put the listener under the tympanum, craning). Eighty metres covers the paving people actually stand on and still stops short of the apse.

anchors.label: Inside
anchors.basis: Under the roof: the nave runs about sixty metres east from the door to the choir; GPS is unreliable inside, so this chapter is offered on the screen and never starts itself.

anchors.label: The east end
anchors.basis: Square Jean-XXIII is the strip you STAND in to look back along the flying buttresses; the view needs the length of the garden, not its gate. Fifty-five metres covers the walk without reaching the parvis (W7.11 defect 16).

name: Ile de la Cite
short_description: The historic island heart of Paris where the city was founded

beats.script_body: Philippe-Auguste confiscated the Jews' possessions, using the proceeds partly to finance Les Halles market, and expelled them from France in 1182. Their centuries-old presence on rue de la Juiverie, the central axis of the Ile de la Cite, came to an end. When he invited the Jews back 16 years later to squeeze them dry once more, they settled on the right bank around rue des Rosiers.
beats.source_passage: Philippe-Auguste had it converted into the church of Sainte-Madeleine; at the same time he confiscated the Jews' possessions

opening_hours_basis: An open Seine island of streets, quays and squares whose value stands in the open, not behind any gate.
visit_basis: Whole Seine island of quays, squares and lanes to walk across between Notre-Dame and Pont Neuf; a setting explored on foot with no single interior to enter here.
judgement_basis: This island is threaded by trafficked streets with quays dropping to the river so a child at speed is unsafe, but it has open squares and benches (place Dauphine, cathedral forecourt) quiet enough to sit and talk, and it stays lit, central and peopled after dark.
queue_basis: This is an open island of streets, bridges, and squares with no gated interior, so there is no line to enter it.

name: Ile Saint-Louis
short_description: A tranquil island of 17th-century classical mansions east of Ile de la Cite

beats.script_body: The Ile Saint-Louis was originally two separate islands: l'Ile Notre-Dame, serving as the cathedral's recreational grounds, and l'Ile aux Vaches, the domain of grazing cows, laundresses and lovers. During the 14th century, a defence tower with a moat divided them. In the first half of the 17th century, the moat was filled in and the two islands united into the Ile Saint-Louis.
beats.source_passage: a defence tower was built on its eastern tip with a moat to its west, which divided it into two

opening_hours_basis: A residential Seine island of open streets and quays freely accessible from the street at any hour.
visit_basis: Small residential island with one main street of 17th-century townhouses, quays and an ice cream stop; the value is walking it, nothing single to enter.
judgement_basis: A residential island whose narrow streets carry cars and whose quays edge straight onto the Seine, so running children are at risk, but its tree-lined quay steps and benches are quiet enough to talk and the streets stay lit and inhabited at night.
queue_basis: A residential island of open streets and shopfronts with no controlled entrance, so nothing is queued before you walk onto it.

name: Hotel de Ville
short_description: Paris's city hall on the site of the medieval Place de Greve

beats.script_body: The municipality of Paris grew from the corporation of water merchants who bought the strand (greve) from Louis VII in the 12th century. A tribunal of commerce was set up on Place de Greve, becoming the embryo of the municipality. The corporation's seal, inherited from the ancient Nautae Parisiaci, remains the coat of arms of Paris with only minor changes a thousand years later.
beats.source_passage: the strand was an invaluable asset to the corporation of water merchants

beats.script_body: Etienne Marcel, provost of Paris, was the first to settle the city government in a town hall on Place de Greve, buying a two-storeyed house from the king on behalf of the city in 1357. Known as La Maison des Piliers for its row of arcades, it was eventually replaced by a magnificent Renaissance building begun under Francois I.
beats.source_passage: Etienne Marcel was the first provost to settle in a town hall on Place de Gréve

beats.script_body: The anti-bourgeois proletarian Commune burnt down the Hotel de Ville in 1871. The victorious bourgeois government of the Third Republic rebuilt it at once in its old style, to brush off this incident and demonstrate that its possession was irrevocable.
beats.source_passage: The anti-bourgeois proletarian Commune, on the other hand, burnt it down in 1871

beats.script_body: Place de Greve served as Paris's main place of public executions, with gallows as a permanent fixture. Notable executions included Cartouche, the terror of early 18th-century Paris; Ravaillac, assassin of Henri IV; and the Marquise de Brinvilliers, mass poisoner.
beats.source_passage: the Place de Gréve is remembered above all as the main place of public executions

beats.script_body: On Friday 17 July 1676, Madame de Sevigne watched the Marquise de Brinvilliers carried to Place de Greve. The Marquise had poisoned her father (requiring ten attempts) and two brothers. Her lover Godin de Sainte-Croix had learned the art of poison from an Italian named Exili while imprisoned in the Bastille. Sevigne wrote: 'At last, it is all over, the Brinvilliers is in the air.'
beats.source_passage: On Friday 17 July 1676, Madame de Sévigné watched the Marquise de Brinvilliers

beats.script_body: Place de Greve was where people gathered in early morning to seek work, a practice called 'faire la greve.' The expression survives in modern French but now means 'to go on strike' — the opposite of its original meaning of seeking employment.
beats.source_passage: The Place de Gréve was also a focal site in the life of the city, where people would gather

beats.script_body: Place de Greve hosted the fete de la Saint-Jean on 24 June, when a 10-metre-high bonfire celebrated the birth of John the Baptist. Occasionally the King himself would come to light the fire, heralded by trumpets.
beats.source_passage: the féte de la Saint-Jean on 24 June, when a 10-metre-high bonfire

opening_hours_basis: Gated building with ticketed exhibition access; transcribed from OSM tag 'Mo-Sa 10:00-19:00' with Sunday closed.
visit_basis: Grand neo-Renaissance city hall facade fronting a large open plaza where you stand back to take in the statues and rooflines; interior open only for occasional booked exhibitions, not a normal visit.
judgement_basis: A city-hall forecourt that is open paved plaza bordered by trafficked streets with no free seating and often fenced for events, so children cannot safely range and there is nowhere to sit quietly, but the square is well lit and peopled into the evening.
queue_basis: The City Hall interior is only open by occasional booked exhibition or event, so a walking-tour stop views the facade and forecourt from the open square with no line.

name: Place des Vosges
short_description: Paris's oldest planned square, surrounded by harmonious brick-and-stone mansions

beats.script_body: Place Royale (now Place des Vosges) was the first open-air square in Paris. Its exquisite bright pink brick and white stone pavilions served in 1612 as the backdrop for the most dazzling celebration recalled by Parisians: the double wedding of Louis XIII and his sister Elisabeth.
physical_cues: pink brick and white stone pavilions
beats.source_passage: This was the first open-air square in Paris

beats.script_body: Place Royale was a favourite site for duels, watched from balconies by ladies whose favours were being sought. Cardinal Richelieu banned duels in 1626. When Boutteville contravened the ruling, believing his glorious pedigree put him above the law, Richelieu had him decapitated at Place de Greve.
physical_cues: Place des Vosges arcades and balconies
beats.source_passage: Place Royale was also a favourite choice for duels

beats.script_body: The Marais in its golden age was studded with magnificent hotels. Great architects Mansart and Le Vau and painters Le Brun, Mignard and Vouet decorated the interiors. The Duc de Richelieu sold ten Nicolas Poussin paintings to Louis XIV and bought some twenty Rubens to replace them.
beats.source_passage: great architects such as Mansart and Le Vau and painters such as Le Brun, Mignard and Vouet

beats.script_body: With the court's transfer to Versailles in 1682, the Marais declined. In 1962, Andre Malraux's rehabilitation bill passed; in 1965 the area was declared a protected zone.
beats.source_passage: With the transfer of the court to Versailles in 1682, the centre of gravity of Paris shifted west

opening_hours_basis: Open public square whose value stands in the open on the pavement, not gated.
visit_basis: Oldest planned square in Paris, 36 uniform brick houses framing a central garden you walk round under the arcades; nothing general to enter, Hugo's house is a separate stop.
judgement_basis: A traffic-free central garden enclosed by uniform arcaded houses with lawns and benches where children can run safely and two people can sit quietly, but the garden itself is railed and gated shut at night.
queue_basis: An open public square entered from the street on all sides with no door or ticket, so there is nothing to queue for.

anchors.label: The garden
anchors.basis: The fenced garden inside the arcades is where the corpus sends a person to find a bench near the children's play area and watch; you stand or sit among the lawns and fountains, not under the arcades. Thirty metres round the centre covers the benches and fountains and stops short of the arcade walks.

name: Centre Pompidou
short_description: Iconic contemporary art centre with inside-out architecture

beats.script_body: Richard Rogers and Renzo Piano designed the Centre Georges Pompidou with bright blue building and bright red and blue piping. Parisians were scandalized that two 'hippy' architects built a 'refinery' in the historic heart of Paris — twenty years later it still ranked first among monuments they wished to see wiped out. Yet it drew 28,000 visitors per day and 8 million per year, beating the Eiffel Tower's 2.5 million.
beats.source_passage: Richard Rogers and Renzo Piano sought to express the spirit of the time

beats.script_body: The Centre Pompidou's piazza became a focal point of Parisian street life, with buskers, acrobats, mime artists, jugglers, fire-eaters, portrait painters and pickpockets spontaneously recreating the medieval atmosphere of the parvis of Notre-Dame.
beats.source_passage: Buskers, acrobats, mime artists, jugglers, fire-eaters, portrait painters and pickpockets share this spacious square

opening_hours_basis: Gated museum; hours from the Centre's own published schedule, closed Tuesdays.
visit_basis: The exposed-pipe exterior and the sloping piazza where crowds gather absorb 20 minutes; inside is Europe's largest modern art collection plus the escalator facade views, which would absorb over two hours, capped at the 90-minute tour maximum.
judgement_basis: The museum interior forbids running, but the large sloping traffic-free forecourt has broad ground and low ledges where people sit and talk, and the plaza is lit and busy with people into the evening, so standing after dark is fine; note the forecourt itself is fairly open, but its slope toward buildings not traffic still does not make it safe free-range running ground for a loud fast child amid dense crowds.
queue_basis: Security screening and ticket gates at the entrance form a modest line at busy afternoon hours, short at opening and near closing.

name: Bibliotheque de l'Arsenal
short_description: Historic library in the former Royal Arsenal, with magnificent Louis XIII interiors and a rich literary heritage.

beats.script_body: Built in the 14th century for ammunition manufacture, the Arsenal lay along an arm of the Seine (now Boulevard Morland). In 1563 a gigantic explosion — heard as far as Melun, 46 km away — blew most of it up. The Duc de Sully built a palatial residence there. Louis XIV later used the abandoned foundry to cast bronze statues for the gardens of Versailles.
beats.source_passage: Built in the 14th century for the manufacture of ammunition, the royal Arsenal

beats.script_body: It was while Henri IV was on his way to the Arsenal from the Louvre, on 14 May 1610, that Ravaillac jumped onto his coach and stabbed him to death.
beats.source_passage: It was in fact while Henri IV was on his way to the Arsenal from the Louvre
beats.fact_check_notes: Date corrected from 10 May to 14 May 1610.

beats.script_body: The Arsenal housed the court of justice where the trial of Nicolas Fouquet, Louis XIV's treasurer, was held in 1664. Despite Colbert's rigged magistrates, the courageous d'Ormesson defied the King's wish for a death sentence and voted for banishment. Louis XIV then commuted the sentence upward to life imprisonment.
beats.source_passage: this was where the scandalous trial of Nicolas Foucquet

beats.script_body: La Voisin's trial in 1680 at the Arsenal was another memorable event. Women of distinction, taking the Marquise de Brinvilliers as a model, set out to eliminate those they found cumbersome. So many names of high-ranking ladies leaked out that procedures were hastened to silence her.
beats.source_passage: La Voisin's trial in 1680 was another memorable event

beats.script_body: Charles Nodier, head of the library from 1824 to 1844, gathered the Romantic writers Victor Hugo, Lamartine, Alfred de Musset, Alexandre Dumas and Sainte-Beuve, perpetuating a 200-year Parisian tradition of salons litteraires.
beats.source_passage: Charles Nodier, the head of the library from 1824 to 1844

beats.script_body: The Arsenal houses the apartment of Madame de Meilleraye, a unique surviving example of a Louis XIII interior. The Marechal de Meilleraye commissioned Simon Vouet to create a dwelling of great splendour for his young bride.
beats.source_passage: The apartment of Madame de Meilleraye provides a unique example of a Louis XIII interior

opening_hours_basis: A historic research library behind doors, gated, but hours not confidently known; left unfiltered.
visit_basis: Historic library in the former Royal Arsenal with Louis XIII period rooms; a short look at the exterior, and access to the show rooms and reading room takes about 25 minutes when open to visitors.
judgement_basis: A historic library where silence is enforced indoors and there is no free public seating for casual talk, and the building is closed and locked after hours.
queue_basis: A working historic library where entry means a reading-room reception or a small guided-visit desk rather than mass ticketing, so at most a few people wait ahead at busy afternoon hours.

name: Pavillon de l'Arsenal
short_description: 19th-century glass-and-steel exhibition space for Paris urbanism and town planning.

beats.script_body: Across from the Arsenal library stands the Pavillon de l'Arsenal, a 19th-century glass and steel structure that served as an art gallery and later as a warehouse of the Samaritaine department store. Since 1988 it has housed temporary exhibitions on different aspects of town planning in Paris.
beats.source_passage: Across the street is the Pavillon de l'Arsenal, a glass and steel structure dating from the 19th century

opening_hours_basis: An exhibition hall entered through doors, gated, but hours not confidently known; left unfiltered.
visit_basis: 19th-century glass-and-steel hall housing Paris urbanism exhibits including a large city model; brief exterior look, and the free galleries absorb around 40 minutes for an engaged visitor.
judgement_basis: A glass-and-steel exhibition hall where quiet browsing is expected and running is not, with no free seating and doors locked at night, leaving no lit open place to stand.
queue_basis: A free urbanism exhibition hall with a single entrance and occasional bag check; a brief line can form on busy weekend afternoons but it clears quickly.
